ideas.risks: The theorem may need small corrections for normalization, zero mass, or strict crossing; the solver's proof might prove only a slightly different support-count convention if support at 0 is mishandled.
ideas.summary: Turn the solver's finite-m result into a polished proposition: for any nonnegative threshold law with at most m positive support points, E[Z] - sup_a a Pr(Z>a) <= ((m-1)/m)^m, with equality for the discrete equal-revenue support. Check every reduction step: removing zero atoms, scaling top support to 1, raising values below rho to rho without increasing rho, preserving support size, using left-limit revenue under strict crossing, and proving tightness from the proposed tail probabilities.
ideas.title: Certify The Finite-m Equal-Revenue Theorem
ideas.why_promising: This is the main new progress in the solver attempt; if accepted, it upgrades CL-023 and supplies a reusable exact constant for all multi-threshold lower-bound lifts.

ideas.risks: The local dual certificate only lower-bounds regret when the common-prefix action law is genuinely shared and outside rewards are capped; otherwise this repeats the failed local-κ-as-standalone mistake.
ideas.summary: Use the finite-m theorem to prove a finite multi-continuation block lemma. For a zero block of length N and terminal continuation c in a chosen m-threshold set C_m, show that every learner with the same zero-block action law across continuations suffers at least N κ(C_m) regret on one continuation, where κ(C_m)=((m-1)/m)^m for the equal-revenue set. Then lift it to the universal/process-unaware dominant-block construction with the old-reward cap M_i.
ideas.title: Finite-m Universal Block Lower Bound
ideas.why_promising: It directly converts the local finite-m geometry into a stronger version of the accepted 1/4 universal block obstruction.

ideas.risks: The limit constant may require choosing m_i and N_i on a delicate diagonal schedule, and the final theorem must not be overstated as instance-wise necessity.
ideas.summary: Diagonalize the finite-m block lower bound with m_i -> infinity and N_i dominating both previous length M_i and any threshold-menu overhead. The target theorem is a universal/process-unaware deterministic block class with limsup R_T/T >= 1/e - o(1), improving the binary 1/4 constant. Verify whether the same construction keeps beta and gamma tails large in the intended sense.
ideas.title: Approach A 1/e Universal Lower Bound
ideas.why_promising: The solver's constant tends to 1/e, matching the accepted continuum κ cap, so this may identify the sharp local minimax obstruction for universal delayed market making.

ideas.risks: Intermediate threshold-round quotes may create extra learner rewards or comparator terms; an O(m) loss is probably safe, but removing it may require careful sup-comparator bookkeeping.
ideas.summary: Prove the same-path multi-threshold lift on deterministic known blocks 0^N,c_1,...,c_m, with regret evaluated after each threshold time. Show that a horizon-oblivious policy's shared zero-block actions imply max_j R_{T_j} >= N κ(C)-M-O(m), and then specialize to equal-revenue C_m. Track exactly how quotes posted at intermediate threshold times affect both learner reward and comparator value.
ideas.title: Multi-Threshold Anytime Prefix Conflict
ideas.why_promising: This would strengthen the accepted known-path horizon-oblivious obstruction from the binary 1/4 case to the finite-m and possibly 1/e regime.

ideas.risks: A local mixed strategy need not compose into a global no-regret algorithm because actions affect many future horizons and censoring changes the payoff matrix over time.
ideas.summary: Derive the primal optimizer for the finite-m zero-block game: find an action distribution μ minimizing sup_c [c - E_{a~μ} a 1{a<c}] for the equal-revenue threshold set, and take the m -> infinity limit. Use small finite LP computations to guess a closed form. Then ask whether this local defensive distribution can be used as a building block for upper bounds in simultaneous-prefix or universal settings.
ideas.title: Find The Primal Equal-Revenue Action Law
ideas.why_promising: The dual constant is valuable, but an explicit primal strategy would clarify sharpness and may point toward matching upper bounds or approachability formulations.

ideas.risks: The resulting condition may become tautological if it just restates regret; it needs either an algorithmic consequence or a clean lower-bound transfer theorem.
ideas.summary: Recast the process-aware horizon-oblivious deterministic-path problem as simultaneous approximation of prefix value functions V_T^*=sup_a sum_{t<=T} r_t(a). Define vector deficits over a moving family of horizons and test whether Blackwell/approachability-style conditions characterize when one action sequence can keep all prefix regrets sublinear. Use sparse vanishing spikes as an easy positive test and multi-threshold blocks as negative tests.
ideas.title: Known-Path Simultaneous-Prefix Framework
ideas.why_promising: It targets the quantifier regime where oracle collapse fails but raw beta-necessity is still false, so it may be the right replacement for tail characterization.

ideas.risks: The construction must avoid being trivialized by horizon-aware oracle policies; it should be stated for expected regret under initial law and with explicit learner information.
ideas.summary: Build a rare-prefix process where, conditional on a rare event, a long multi-threshold block has κ close to 1/e, but the event probability p_i makes p_i N_i=o(T). Show that essential-sup or conditional κ tails remain large while expected regret is small for a simple process-aware policy. This would formalize the rare-history obstruction with the sharper finite-m gadget.
ideas.title: Rare Multi-Threshold Prefix Stress Test
ideas.why_promising: It would clarify why any information-tail necessity must be frequency-weighted, not based on essential sup or unweighted local hardness.

ideas.risks: The exact finite-m constant may not appear in the literature under the same normalization, so the search can return only adjacent terminology rather than a citation.
ideas.summary: Search the price-discrimination, robust pricing, and buyer-optimal signaling literature for the exact finite-support problem: maximize E[Z]-sup_a a Pr(Z>a) over m-point laws on [0,1]. Compare the solver proof with discrete equal-revenue distributions, finite-signal buyer-optimal schemes, and minimax pricing duals; report whether the result is known, a corollary, or apparently new.
ideas.title: Check Whether CL-023 Is Known
ideas.why_promising: A citation or known formulation would strengthen the final writeup and prevent duplicating an existing finite-support monopoly-pricing theorem.
